Fentanyl and naloxone. Fentanyl is a fully synthetic opioid: it is made in a lab, not taken from the poppy, so strictly it is not an alkaloid. You can still classify both of its nitrogens. The N in its six-membered ring is a tertiary (3°) amine, the basic group that lets it be given as a salt (fentanyl citrate). The other N is a tertiary amide: it is bonded to the C=O carbon, a benzene ring and a ring carbon, so it carries no H. In California, fentanyl was involved in 7,137 overdose deaths in 2023.1 Naloxone (Narcan) rapidly reverses an opioid overdose, and on March 29, 2023, the FDA approved the 4 mg nasal spray for sale without a prescription,2 so nurses and dental hygienists may be the ones who show patients and families how to use it.

Sources: 1. California Department of Public Health, Opioid-Related Overdose Deaths in California, 2023, 2025. 2. U.S. Food and Drug Administration, FDA Approves First Over-the-Counter Naloxone Nasal Spray, 2023.

Valley Connection: Garlic, Onions and the Smell of Sulfur

Whole garlic and onions smell mild. Cutting or crushing them breaks the cells and lets an enzyme turn odorless sulfur compounds into volatile ones, including small thiols, and that is the sharp smell you notice. California grows most of the nation’s garlic (86%, by a 2007 UC Davis estimate), including fields in the Valley counties of Fresno, Kern and Kings.1 In 2022 the state’s garlic crop was worth $309 million, and California supplies 99% or more of the garlic the United States exports.2

The connection. Your nose picks up thiols at extremely low concentrations. That is exactly why a thiol is the warning odor added to natural gas and propane (above): the “gas smell” and the garlic smell are both the –SH group at work.

Sources: 1. UC Davis News, Natural Fungicide Gives Garlic Growers Hope, 2007. 2. California Department of Food and Agriculture, California Agricultural Statistics Review 2022–2023, 2023.

Valley Connection: Beans and Corn Tortillas

A plate of beans with corn tortillas is a classic pair of complementary proteins. Corn (maize) protein is low in two essential amino acids, lysine and tryptophan. Bean protein is a good source of lysine and tryptophan but is low in the sulfur-containing amino acids, such as methionine.1 Each food fills in what the other lacks, so eaten together they give the amino acid pool a much better balance of the essential amino acids, the ones the body cannot make (Section 15.11).1 This matters for patients who eat little meat, eggs or dairy, whether by choice, by budget or by tradition.

Sources: 1. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Maize in Human Nutrition, Chapter 8: Improvement of maize diets, 1992.

Valley Connection: Every California Newborn Gets the Heel Stick

California law requires that every baby born in the state be screened; parents may decline only if screening conflicts with their religious beliefs or practices.1 Between 12 and 48 hours after birth, a provider takes a few drops of blood from the baby’s heel onto a blood-spot card, which goes to a state-contracted laboratory.1 The California Newborn Screening Program tests for more than 80 serious but treatable conditions,1 including PKU, sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, classic galactosemia and congenital hypothyroidism.2 About 1 in every 600 newborns tested is diagnosed with one of them.1 A positive screen is not a diagnosis: it means the baby needs more testing to confirm whether the condition is really there.1

Valley Connection: Folic Acid in the Tortilla

The folate row of the vitamin table lists neural-tube defects. As THF, folate carries the one-carbon units used to make nucleotides, so the fast-dividing cells of an embryo need plenty of it very early in pregnancy. CDC notes that Hispanic/Latina women have a high risk of having a baby with a neural-tube defect.1 In 2016 the FDA allowed folic acid to be added to corn masa flour on a voluntary basis,2 but CDC reports that, in data from 2011–2020, voluntary fortification had not yet improved folate levels among Hispanic/Latina women.1

California’s law. AB 1830, signed September 28, 2024, made fortification required: starting January 1, 2026, corn masa flour made, sold or used in California must contain 0.7 mg of folic acid per pound, and wet corn masa products may contain 0.4 mg per pound.3 Masa is the dough behind corn tortillas and tamales, so a staple food now carries the vitamin.

Sources: 1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Improving Folic Acid Intake, accessed 2026. 2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Folic Acid: Sources and Recommended Intake, accessed 2026. 3. Valley Connection: Plastics on the Farm

Walk past a Valley field and you will see addition polymers everywhere. Growers lay polyethylene mulch film over planting beds to control weeds and help yields,1 water rows through thin plastic drip tape,1 and carry irrigation water in PVC pipe. Both polymers come from the reaction in the table: polyethylene from ethylene (ethene), CH2=CH2, and poly(vinyl chloride) from vinyl chloride (chloroethene), CH2=CHCl. Their backbones are all C–C single bonds, with no ester or amide links for water to hydrolyze, so they last for seasons in sun and soil; used mulch film and drip tape can be collected and recycled.1

Sources: 1. NOAA, Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, Agricultural Field Plastics, accessed 2026.

Valley Connection: Propane Tanks in the Country

Many rural homes, farms and shops in the Valley are not on a natural-gas line and run on propane from a tank. In Fresno County about 14,400 households, 4.3% of occupied homes, heat mainly with bottled, tank or LP gas, compared with 2.9% statewide.1 Propane, C3H8 (44 g/mol), is heavier than air (about 29 g/mol on average), so a leak does not rise and drift out a window the way methane does. It sinks, spreads along the floor, and collects in basements, crawl spaces, ditches and other low spots until it can reach a mixture that will ignite. The thiol odorant added to propane (Section 4.9) is what lets you smell it first.

Sources: 1. U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 1-year estimates, Table B25040 (House Heating Fuel), via Census Reporter, accessed 2026.

Clinical Connection: Nursing

Absorbable and nonabsorbable sutures. The ester-versus-amide difference decides how long a stitch lasts. Polyglycolic acid sutures are a polyester: water in tissue fluid hydrolyzes their ester bonds, the strand gradually loses strength and is absorbed, and no one has to take it out.1 Nylon sutures are a polyamide. Amides are much harder to hydrolyze than esters (Section 7.7), so nylon is a nonabsorbable suture: it stays in the tissue until it is removed.2 When you chart a wound closure, the suture type tells you whether a removal visit is needed.

Sources: 1. Szabelski J, Karpiński R, Short-Term Hydrolytic Degradation of Mechanical Properties of Absorbable Surgical Sutures: A Comparative Study, J Funct Biomater, 2024. 2. Melega MV, et al., Comparison Between Nylon and Polyglactin Sutures in Pediatric Cataract Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial, Front Med, 2021.

Example 3: Read the enzyme panel

Problem. Use the table to name the damaged tissue in each patient. (a) A 58-year-old with crushing chest pain has a rising troponin I and a high CK-MB. (b) A student who took far too much acetaminophen has very high ALT and AST. (c) A patient with severe pain in the upper abdomen has high lipase and amylase.

Solution. (a) Heart. Troponin is the most specific cardiac marker, and CK-MB is the heart form of creatine kinase, so the panel points to a myocardial infarction (MI, heart attack). (b) Liver. ALT is mostly in liver, and the table lists acetaminophen overdose among the causes of a rise in ALT and AST. (c) Pancreas. Lipase and amylase are pancreatic hydrolases that digest fat and starch, and they rise in acute pancreatitis.

Check. Match each enzyme to where it lives, not just to the symptom. A high LDH alone could not answer any of these, because LDH is found in nearly every tissue and is not specific.

Example: Reading the anion gap in DKA

Problem. A patient with type 1 diabetes arrives with fruity breath and deep, rapid breathing. The lab reports Na+ 138, Cl− 100 and HCO3− 10 (all in mEq/L). Calculate the anion gap and explain what fills it.

Solution. The anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = 138 − (100 + 10) = 28 mEq/L. A typical value is about 12, and DKA is diagnosed with a gap above about 10 to 12 (each lab sets its own normal range).1,2 Blood must have equal positive and negative charge, so a large gap means negative ions the panel does not measure. In DKA these are the carboxylate ions of the ketone bodies acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate. Each ketone acid that releases H+ uses up a bicarbonate, which is why the HCO3− fell to 10 while the gap grew.1

Check. Acetone is not counted: it has no acid group and no charge (see the Think about it question above).

Sources: 1. MSD Manual Professional Version, Acid-Base Disorders, accessed 2026. 2. MSD Manual Professional Version, Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), accessed 2026.
